newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan people back cautious China policy.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan people back cautious China policy.

text.p: The majority of Taiwan people support their government's tough stance on investment in rival China, saying the island has become too dependent on its giant neighbour, a government survey said on Wednesday.

The survey, conducted by the economics ministry, showed that an overwhelming 94 percent of 2,000 respondents felt national security should be Taipei's top consideration in making its economic and trade policies toward the mainland.

Eighty-four percent said Taipei should regulate investments in China by local businesses, and 96 percent agreed that investment projects in the mainland by big-capital Taiwan firms should be restricted.
The results appeared to support the government's policy that urges local companies to "refrain from temptation" and put national interest before their own when considering investments in China.
Another recent state-financed survey showed more than half of Taiwan firms have suffered losses in their investments in China.
Officials declined to say whether the surveys were aimed at dissuading Taiwan companies from investing in the mainland.

Taiwan, separated from China at the end of a civil war in 1949, bans direct contact and investment on the mainland. All investments must be approved by the government and routed through Hong Kong or other third places.
Amid recent strained ties, Taiwan has expressed concern that its economy may become too dependent on China, thus becoming politically vulnerable.
In a prepared keynote address to the National Assembly, President Lee Teng-hui asked Taiwan businesses to comply with the government's policies.

"Before the hostility across the Taiwan Strait is removed... local businesses and industries should realise that the country's survival and development are far more important than business opportunity," Lee said.
Lee was scheduled to deliver the speech on Tuesday but was kept from the podium by an opposition filibuster.

The ministry's survey also showed that 58 percent of Taiwan people said Taiwan's investments in China have grown too fast over the past years, while 65 percent said rapidly increasing mainland investments would have a negative impact on the island's economy.
Some 30,000 companies from Taiwan, which China regards as a renegade province, have poured more than US$30 billion into the mainland since an unofficial thaw began in the 1980s.
Taiwan recently drafted a set of criteria to govern local investment in China.

Under pressure from Taiwan government, Formosa Plastics said on May 7 that it would abandon a US$3 billion China power plant project if Taiwan keeps its plan to ban firms from investing in utilities and public works there.
Some 70 percent of the people surveyed by the ministry said the government should continue to ban local manufactures from investing in high-technology and basic infrastructure in China.
Analysts have said Taiwan companies could easily -- and legally -- dodge the government's tightening policy by conducting their mainland investments through overseas affiliates.
They expect more companies to take that approach if the government's stance shows no signs of easing.
